name: Topshine
what: Direct a whole AI film for the price of a coffee. Topshine plans every shot with several takes, renders them all at once, and lets you pick the best and finish the film in a full editor.
glance: Up to 90% cheaper than closed video APIs
Several takes of every shot, rendered at once on rented GPUs
A capped quote on every job; pay only for clips made
34 transitions, auto-captions, beat-synced music and social presets
archHi:
Topshine is a hosted video studio on open-weights video models. It rents an RTX 5090 for each session of work and charges for the machine time the clips take.

  1. Plan. Write each shot once, with as many takes as you want.
  2. Render. Every take renders in one batch, on rented GPUs running open video models.
  3. Pick. Choose the best take for each shot.
  4. Finish. Cut, caption and score the film, then export it for any platform.

When the session ends, the customer pays what the made clips cost, up to the cap. Failed clips cost nothing, a machine that fails its checks is replaced at the service's expense, and the rest of the hold returns to the balance.
arch:
The engine is videogen, a Python library that rents GPUs from live offers and drives the video models on them. Topshine vendors it unchanged and wraps it in accounts, credits, storage, a session queue, screens, email and operations.

  • Offers come from a snapshot. A supervisor fetches RTX 5090 offers from Vast.ai, RunPod and CloudRift every 60 seconds. Quotes and Confirm read that snapshot only while it is under two minutes old, so no customer request waits on a provider's feed.
  • Two figures per quote. The expected price is the cheapest offer's typical estimate. The cap is the highest estimate among the three cheapest offers. The quote stores its offers and their rates, and a machine whose rate has risen since is skipped.
  • The cap fixes the paid time. A machine's deadline is set from the cap when it is created and is never extended. Clips added mid-session are accepted only while the queue still fits before that deadline, so an addition needs no second hold. A file lock on the session's queue settles the race between an addition and the run closing.
  • Waiting has a limit. When no offer fits the cap, the session waits and tries again every 5 minutes. After 30 minutes it fails and the hold is released in full.
  • Credits move through a ledger. Purchases, holds, settlements, releases, refunds and adjustments are ledger rows, each with an idempotency key. Balances change in the same transaction under a row lock, and database constraints refuse an overdraw. A nightly task checks every balance against the ledger's sums and alerts on any difference.
  • The charge follows the made clips. A session costs the GPU time of its made clips plus a share of the machine's startup, model download and idle time, in proportion to the generating time those clips took. Failed clips, and sessions that made nothing, are booked to the service.
  • One task settles a session. Every path that ends a run queues the same settlement task under one key, so a session settles exactly once, whichever process noticed the end first. On restart the supervisor finds sessions whose process died by their free session lock, and settles them.
  • The engine's ledger file is the record. Each engine row is appended to the session's own file first and mirrored to Postgres through a spool that retries every 10 seconds. The settlement re-imports the file before it computes, so a database outage mid-run loses no charge.

Every rented machine is watched while it works:

CheckWhenOn a fail
Download guardduring the 61 GB model downloadafter two slow windows in a row the machine is ended and the next offer is tried, at the service's cost
Pace checkwhile clips runa clip over 1.5× its expected time ends the session on the clips made, and Retry quotes the rest
Destroy and verifyat the end of every sessiona sweep every 10 minutes destroys any machine past its deadline, and an unverified destroy alerts the operator
  • Bad hosts are remembered. A machine that fails a check ranks last for 14 days, for every account.
  • Retries skip what cannot change. A failed clip gets a second pass while the machine is still up. Out of memory at that length, a refused input and a passed deadline are never retried.
  • Accounts are sealed off. Every table carries the account, with row-level security, and an id that belongs to another account answers 404, the same as one that does not exist.
proc:
• One Python container with two processes. Python 3.12 on Railway. A FastAPI web process serves the screens, the /v1 API and the Stripe and Clerk webhooks. A supervisor runs the session loop, the task pools and the schedules, and each session runs in its own subprocess that drives the engine on a rented RTX 5090. Postgres on Supabase holds accounts, money, sessions and clips through plain psycopg and numbered SQL migrations. Plan files live on a volume and finished clips in Cloudflare R2. Sign-in is Clerk, payments are Stripe Checkout and email is Resend.
  • Ports and adapters at the engine boundary. The engine takes its side effects as injected hooks: the ledger writer, the cancel check, the queue refresh and close, and the alert sink. Topshine supplies its own, and every hook's default keeps the standalone tool's behaviour, so the same engine runs both.
  • An explicit state machine with guarded transitions. A session moves through queued, starting, running and finishing to one of four end states. Each move is a conditional update that matches only from the expected state, so when a cancel and the supervisor's start race for the same session, exactly one wins.
  • A transactional work queue in Postgres. Sessions and background tasks are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and each task carries a unique key, so a retried or duplicated task does nothing.
  • Idempotency at every entry point. Stripe webhooks are deduplicated by event id, API writes take an Idempotency-Key header, and ledger rows and emails carry unique keys. A retry anywhere writes nothing twice.
  • An append-only log with a replayable projection. The engine's per-session usage file is the source of truth for billing. The ledger, clip and machine rows in Postgres are a projection of it, which the settlement rebuilds before it computes.
  • Reconciliation as a scheduled job. Nightly, every account's balances are recomputed from the credit ledger and compared, and a mismatch alerts the operator.
